impede

im-PEED -- Latin impedire, literally 'to shackle the feet' (pes, pedis, 'foot'). · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To impede is to slow down or make progress difficult.

Officials feared the endless paperwork would impede the relief effort more than the weather did.

Worked Example

A marathon runner keeps moving through the storm, but the headwind and ankle-deep puddles cut her pace nearly in half, mile after mile.

She is still moving forward -- just far more slowly. That dragging, slowing effect is exactly what it means to impede progress; a blocked course that stopped her entirely would be obstructed instead.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

hamper: To hamper is to restrict or entangle movement or effort, the way a heavy coat hampers a climber. Impede covers any drag on progress, large or small, while hamper pictures something wrapped around you, snagging and tangling as you keep moving.

hinder: To hinder is to create difficulties that hold a person or plan back from succeeding. Impede points at forward motion being dragged slower, while hinder is broader -- you can hinder a career or a friendship that is not literally moving anywhere.

delay: To delay is to push something to a later time than planned -- the flight leaves, but two hours late. To impede is different: the effort keeps going the whole time, only slower. A delay costs you the start; an impeded effort crawls on.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

expedite: to speed a process up

facilitate: to make something easier

Where it sits · how much drag the obstacle creates — slow → impede → cripple

slow vs. impede: Slow is the mildest word on this scale and much weaker than impede -- anything can slow something a little, while impede means a real obstacle is dragging hard against its progress.

cripple vs. impede: Cripple is far stronger than impede: an impeded effort still grinds forward against the drag, while a crippled one is damaged so badly it can barely function at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — im-

Prefix — im-: in, on (the form in- takes before p) (Latin)

Root — pede

Root — pede: foot (from Latin pes, pedis -- the same root spelled ped- in pedestrian and pedal, and pede in centipede)

Put it together

Put it together: Im- ('in, on' -- the shape in- takes before p) + pede ('foot', from Latin pes, pedis) spell impede. Latin impedire meant 'to shackle the feet', so to impede progress is to hobble its feet -- the same root that gives us pedestrian and pedal. Its opposite, expedite, literally means to free the feet.

Use the root in a new word: pedestrian

Use the root in a new word: pedestrian: A pedestrian waited at the crosswalk for the light to change.

Root Check

Word Choice

Impede means to slow or hamper progress -- 'impede traffic,' 'impede recovery' -- while this unit's obstruct means to block the way entirely. Rain can impede a rescue that a collapsed tunnel would obstruct.
